blocks.text: It was now late in the afternoon, and sunset was not far off. We had to admit that we had failed. Feeling very sad, we agreed with the Professor when he said:

“Let us go back to Madam Mina—poor, poor dear Madam Mina. We have done all we can do right now. At least we can protect her there. But we do not need to lose hope. There is only one more earth-box, and we must try to find it. When that is done, everything may still be all right.” I could see that he spoke as bravely as he could to comfort Harker. The poor man was completely broken. From time to time, he let out a low groan that he could not hold back. He was thinking of his wife.

With sad hearts, we came back to my house and found Mrs. Harker waiting for us. She put on a cheerful look that showed how brave and unselfish she was. When she saw our faces, her own face turned as pale as death. For a second or two, her eyes closed as if she were praying silently. Then she said cheerfully:

“I can never thank you all enough. Oh, my poor darling!” As she spoke, she took her husband’s grey head in her hands and kissed it. “Lay your poor head here and rest it. Everything will still be all right, dear! God will protect us if that is His good purpose.” The poor man groaned. His misery was too deep and overwhelming for words.

We had supper together without much interest, and I think it cheered us all up a little. Perhaps it was just the simple physical warmth that food gives to hungry bodies, because none of us had eaten anything since breakfast. Or perhaps being together as friends helped us. In any case, we all felt less miserable, and tomorrow no longer seemed completely without hope. True to our promise, we told Mrs. Harker everything that had happened. At times, she turned as white as snow when danger had seemed to threaten her husband. At other times, she turned red when the story showed his deep love and loyalty to her. Even so, she listened bravely and calmly. When we came to the part where Harker had rushed at the Count without thinking of the danger, she grabbed her husband’s arm and held it tight. She held on as if that could protect him from any harm that might come. However, she said nothing until we had finished the whole story and brought everything up to the present moment. Then, without letting go of her husband’s hand, she stood up among us and spoke. Oh, I wish I could give you some idea of that scene! There stood that sweet, sweet, good, good woman, shining with the beauty of her youth and lively spirit. On her forehead was the red scar. She knew it was there. When we looked at it, we ground our teeth, remembering where it had come from and how it happened. Her loving kindness stood against our dark hate. Her gentle faith stood against all our fears and doubts. And we knew that, as far as symbols went, she was cast out from God—even with all her goodness, purity, and faith.

“Jonathan,” she said. The word sounded like music on her lips, because it was so full of love and tenderness. “Jonathan dear, and all of you, my true, true friends, I want you to keep something in mind through all this terrible time. I know that you must fight. You must destroy, just as you destroyed the false Lucy so that the true Lucy might live on after death. But this is not a work of hate. That poor soul who has caused all this misery is the saddest case of all. Just think how joyful he will be when his worse part is destroyed too, so that his better part may live forever in spirit. You must feel pity for him, too, even though it must not stop you from destroying him.”

As she spoke, I could see her husband’s face grow dark and tight. It looked as if the fierce feeling inside him were shrinking his whole self down to its centre. Without thinking, his grip on his wife’s hand grew tighter until his knuckles looked white. She did not pull back from the pain that I knew she must be feeling. Instead, she looked at him with eyes that begged him more deeply than ever. As she stopped speaking, he jumped to his feet, almost tearing his hand away from hers as he spoke:
